title: Automated Release Channels
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of automated release channels and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to automated release channels.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on automated release channels. Release channels distinguish stable releases, prereleases, and release candidates; each channel needs explicit version and publication rules. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Automated Release Channels matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Release channels distinguish stable releases, prereleases, and release candidates; each channel needs explicit version and publication rules. Publishing is a supply-chain boundary. content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Release channels distinguish stable releases, prereleases, and release candidates; each channel needs explicit version and publication rules. Publishing is a supply-chain boundary. Make versions traceable to source commits, authenticate with scoped credentials, record provenance where supported, and validate artifacts before promotion. The most useful check is one that produces observable evidence and fails clearly when its stated requirement is not met.

items.title: Stable releases
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.title: Prereleases
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.title: Release candidate workflows
items.text: Match the event to the intended lifecycle, then test positive and negative branch/path/activity cases. Event payloads may be attacker-controlled, and scheduled jobs use UTC rather than a guaranteed exact start time.

items.title: Version tagging
items.text: Use filters to reduce unnecessary runs only when skipped work is genuinely unrelated. Include shared dependencies and test the changed and unchanged path cases so required checks are not bypassed.

items.title: Changelog generation
items.text: Start with the first failed step and its exit code, then inspect the event, conditions, permissions, tool versions, network, and runner state. Capture sanitized diagnostics and preserve evidence of the failure.

items.title: Package distribution
items.text: Trace the release to a source commit, validate the selected version/ref, restrict publication permissions, retain build evidence, and verify the published artifact before promoting it.

items.title: Release artifact integrity
items.text: Use an artifact for a file produced by a run, choose exact upload/download paths, set retention intentionally, and verify the downloaded file is from the intended run/job.

content_blocks.code:
name: Validate release candidate
on:
  push:
    tags: ["v*.*.*-rc.*"]
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  candidate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: echo "Run compatibility tests and prepare candidate notes"
content_blocks.expected_output: Tags matching the release-candidate pattern trigger validation, not a stable publication.
content_blocks.run_instructions: Create a test tag in a sandbox and confirm only candidate validation runs.
content_blocks.reset_steps: Define separately how an approved release candidate is promoted to a stable release.

content_blocks.title: Practice and verification
content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to automated release channels. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. Record the difference between your prediction and the actual result. Do not add production secrets or grant write permissions just to make a sample pass.

items.title: Syntax and scope
items.text: Check YAML indentation and confirm whether the setting belongs at workflow, job, or step level.

items.title: Permissions and trust
items.text: Start with read-only access. If the example needs more access, explain the exact operation and reduce permissions again afterwards.

items.title: Evidence
items.text: Use the run summary and first failing step. A green result is meaningful only when the intended checks actually ran.

content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain automated release channels, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Publish packages and container images with traceable versions and integrity checks.

content.task: Apply automated release channels to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.
task_acceptance_criteria: Identify the relevant event, workflow field, runner behavior, or security boundary.
Explain the expected success result and at least one failure or skip condition.
Use least privilege and a disposable/test context; do not include credentials or production resources.
hints: Start with the key behavior: Release channels distinguish stable releases, prereleases, and release candidates; each channel needs explicit version and publication rules.
Inspect the exact event filters, permissions, expressions, inputs, and job dependencies that affect this example.
Compare the observed status and logs with the expected result; distinguish static validation from a real hosted run.
content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Release channels distinguish stable releases, prereleases, and release candidates; each channel needs explicit version and publication rules. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
summary: Release channels distinguish stable releases, prereleases, and release candidates; each channel needs explicit version and publication rules.
Publishing is a supply-chain boundary. Make versions traceable to source commits, authenticate with scoped credentials, record provenance where supported, and validate artifacts before promotion.
Use the provided example as a starting point, replace placeholders with repository-specific checks, and validate both success and expected failure behavior before publication.
